questions.stem: A pack of 52 cards consists of four suits with 13 cards in each suit.

parts.stem: i. One card is drawn from the pack and kept on the table. A second card is drawn and placed beside it on the table. What is the probability that the second card is from a different suit to the first?
parts.hint: After the first card is drawn, 51 cards remain. Three suits different from the first suit contain 39 cards.

steps.explain: The first card can be any suit. Once it is on the table, 3 of the 4 suits are different from its suit, giving 39 suitable cards among 51 remaining.
Simplify the fraction.

parts.stem: ii. The two cards are replaced and the pack shuffled. Four cards are chosen from the pack and placed side by side on the table. What is the probability that these four cards are all from different suits?
parts.hint: After the first card, each next card must come from a suit not yet represented: 39, then 26, then 13 suitable cards remain.

questions.stem: A chessboard has 32 black squares and 32 white squares. Tanya chooses three different squares at random.

parts.stem: i. What is the probability that Tanya chooses three white squares?
parts.hint: The three squares are selected without replacement. Multiply the white-square probabilities as the total and white counts decrease.

steps.explain: There are 32 white squares among 64. If the first is white, 31 white remain among 63, then 30 among 62.
Simplify the product.

parts.stem: ii. What is the probability that the three squares Tanya chooses are the same colour?
parts.hint: Three squares are the same colour if all are white or all are black. The two probabilities are equal.

steps.explain: By symmetry, all-black has the same probability as all-white, which is 5/42 from part i. These two events are disjoint.
Add.

parts.stem: iii. What is the probability that the three squares Tanya chooses are not the same colour?
parts.hint: Use the complement of “all three are the same colour.”

steps.explain: The same-colour probability from part ii is 5/21.
Subtract from 1.

Multiply by 6 and simplify.

questions.stem: In a game, a turn involves rolling two dice, each with faces marked 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. The score for each turn is calculated by multiplying the two numbers uppermost on the dice.

parts.stem: i. What is the probability of scoring zero on the first turn?
parts.hint: A product is zero if either die shows 0. Use the complement: subtract the chance that both dice are non-zero.

steps.explain: There are six equally likely faces on each die, including zero. A non-zero face has probability 5/6.
The score is zero in every other case: at least one die shows zero.

parts.stem: ii. What is the probability of scoring 16 or more on the first turn?
parts.hint: List products at least 16 using faces 0 to 5. The ordered pairs are (4,4), (4,5), (5,4) and (5,5).

steps.explain: There are 36 ordered outcomes because each of the two dice has 6 faces. Products at least 16 require both faces to be 4 or 5.
There are four favourable outcomes. Divide by 36.

parts.stem: iii. What is the probability that the sum of the scores in the first two turns is less than 45?
parts.hint: Find the complement: a total of 45 or more can only happen if one turn scores 25 and the other scores 20, or both score 25.

steps.explain: A turn’s largest possible product is 25 (5×5). To reach a total of at least 45, the two scores must be 25 and 20, 20 and 25, or 25 and 25.
There is 1 ordered dice outcome for score 25 and 2 for score 20, out of 36 outcomes per turn. Across two turns, the complement therefore has 1×2 + 2×1 + 1×1 = 5 ordered outcomes out of 36×36.
Subtract from 1.

questions.hint: A score is a product on each turn. For part iii, use the maximum score of 25 and count the few exceptional totals that are not less than 45.

questions.stem: A magician has three 6-sided dice: one always shows 6 (biased), one has \(P(\text{even})=0.8\) (biased), and one is fair. A die is selected at random and rolled, showing an even number. What is the probability that it was one of the two biased dice?
questions.hint: Use Bayes' theorem: \(P(\text{biased}\mid\text{even})=\dfrac{P(\text{biased}\cap\text{even})}{P(\text{even})}\), building both from the full probability tree (each die chosen with probability \(\frac13\)).

steps.explain: Find \(P(\text{even})\) by adding the even-probability of each die, each weighted by \(\frac13\) (chance of selecting it).
Find \(P(\text{biased die}\cap\text{even})\), using only the two biased dice.
Divide to apply Bayes' theorem.

questions.stem: Pat and Chandra take turns rolling two fair dice. The first player to roll a double six wins, and Pat goes first. If they keep playing until someone wins, what is the probability Pat eventually wins?

keyPoints.text: double six
keyPoints.note: Pat succeeds on a turn with probability \(p=1/36\), and fails with probability \(q=35/36\).

keyPoints.text: Pat goes first
keyPoints.note: For Pat to win on his kth turn, each earlier pair of turns must contain two failures.

keyPoints.text: eventually wins
keyPoints.note: Sum the infinite geometric series of Pat-win paths; its ratio is \(q^2\), since each full round has two failures.

steps.explain: A Pat-win path starts with success at his first turn, or with two failures before his next turn.
Each additional round requires two more failures, so consecutive terms have ratio q squared.
Since q squared is less than one, apply the convergent infinite geometric sum.

questions.stem: A bag contains two red balls, one black ball, and one white ball. Andrew selects one ball from the bag and keeps it hidden. He then selects a second ball, also keeping it hidden.

parts.stem: Draw a tree diagram to show all the possible outcomes.
parts.hint: Start with the first draw: red has probability 2/4, black 1/4, and white 1/4. After each branch, there are three balls left; reduce the count of the colour drawn first.

steps.explain: At the first draw there are 4 balls: two red (R), one black (B), and one white (W). These are the first branches.

The ball is not replaced. After a red first draw, one red, one black and one white remain. After a black first draw, two red and one white remain. After a white first draw, two red and one black remain.
The completed tree has three branches after R, two after B, and two after W. Each path shows an ordered pair of colours; branch probabilities on a path multiply.
steps.work: \(RR, RB, RW;\quad BR, BW;\quad WR, WB\)

keyPoints.note: The first draw has 3 colour branches; the second draw changes because the first ball is not replaced.

parts.answer: Tree diagram showing all possible ordered colour outcomes.

parts.stem: Find the probability that both the selected balls are red.
parts.hint: For two reds without replacement, the first draw is red from 2 of 4 balls; then only 1 red remains among 3 balls.

steps.explain: There are 2 red balls among 4 at the first draw. After taking one red, 1 red remains among 3 balls.
Multiply the probabilities along the red-then-red path.

keyPoints.text: Find the probability that both the selected balls are red
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition to choose the appropriate probability calculation.

parts.stem: Find the probability that at least one of the selected balls is red.
parts.hint: It is quicker to find the opposite event: neither selected ball is red. There are only the black and white balls that can be drawn.

steps.explain: Use the complement. “At least one red” is the opposite of “no red”. The two non-red balls are one black and one white.
For no red, the first ball must be black or white (2 of 4), then the other non-red ball is 1 of the 3 remaining.
Subtract this from 1.

keyPoints.text: Find the probability that at least one of the selected balls is red
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition to choose the appropriate probability calculation.

parts.stem: Andrew drops one of the selected balls and we can see that it is red. What is the probability that the ball that is still hidden is also red?
parts.hint: Treat the two draws as ordered: red-red, red-black, red-white, black-red, and white-red are the possible colour sequences once we know a red ball was selected. They are equally likely.

steps.explain: The two balls are selected in order and are not replaced. Each of the five colour sequences containing at least one red has probability 1/6: RR, RB, RW, BR or WR.
The visible red condition leaves exactly these five equally likely sequences. Only RR means the ball still hidden is red.

keyPoints.text: we can see that it is red
keyPoints.note: This observation restricts the possible two-draw colour sequences to those containing a red ball.

questions.stem: Greg and Jack are playing in a golf tournament. They will play two rounds and each has an equal chance of winning the first round. If Greg wins the first round, his probability of winning the second round is increased to 0.6. If Greg loses the first round, his probability of winning the second round is reduced to 0.3.

parts.stem: Draw a tree diagram for the two-round sequence. Label each branch of the diagram with the appropriate probability.
parts.hint: Start with Greg win/lose in round 1, each with probability 0.5. Then use the stated conditional probabilities for round 2.

steps.explain: In round 1, Greg wins or loses with equal probability. Those two branches add to 1.
If he wins round 1, the round-2 branches are win 0.6 and lose 0.4. If he loses round 1, the round-2 branches are win 0.3 and lose 0.7.
A complete tree has four endpoints: WW, WL, LW and LL. Multiply along each path to find its probability.

parts.stem: Find the probability that Greg wins exactly one round.
parts.hint: Exactly one win can happen in two orders: win then lose, or lose then win. Add those two path probabilities.

steps.explain: There are two ways to win exactly one round: WL or LW.
Multiply along each path using the tree probabilities.
The two paths cannot happen together, so add them.

parts.hint: At the first choice, 4 of the 12 chocolates are hard.

steps.explain: There are 4 hard chocolates among 12 total chocolates before any are eaten.

keyPoints.text: the first chocolate Kim eats is hard
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition to choose the appropriate probability calculation.

parts.stem: Kim eats three hard chocolates;
parts.hint: The chocolates are not replaced: multiply 4/12, then 3/11, then 2/10.

steps.explain: For three hard chocolates in a row without replacement, the hard count and total count each drop after every hard chocolate.
Multiply and reduce the fraction.

keyPoints.text: Kim eats three hard chocolates
keyPoints.note: Use this exact condition to choose the appropriate probability calculation.

parts.stem: Kim eats exactly one hard chocolate.
parts.hint: Exactly one hard chocolate can appear in three positions: HSS, SHS or SSH. Find one path, then multiply by 3.

steps.explain: First calculate one order, HSS. The probability of hard then soft then soft changes because there is no replacement.
The single hard chocolate can be first, second or third. Each order has the same probability because it uses one hard and two soft draws.
